Page two: history. Video games go back to the early nineteen fifties, when computer scientists in universities designed simple games as part of their research, or just for fun.
In the nineteen sixties, students at M I T played games on huge university computers. Moves were often fed in using punched cards, which are cards with holes in them the computer could read.
Gaming didn't go mainstream until the nineteen seventies and eighties, with arcade games, home consoles and home computers.
The game most often called the first video game is Tennis for Two, from October nineteen fifty-eight.
It was created by William Higinbotham, a physicist at Brookhaven National Laboratory in New York, with technician Robert Dvorak, who built it.
And it wasn't made to make money. It was made to entertain visitors at the laboratory's open day, and show that science could be fun.
It showed a side view of a tennis court on a small round oscilloscope screen. Each player had a controller box with a knob to set the angle of their shot, and a button to hit the ball.
There was no score on screen. Players kept score themselves. And hundreds of visitors queued to play it.
Other early games: OXO, from nineteen fifty-two, which was noughts and crosses against the computer at Cambridge University. Players chose squares with a rotary telephone dial.
Spacewar, from nineteen sixty-two, a two-player spaceship battle made at M I T. And Pong, from nineteen seventy-two, Atari's table tennis arcade game and the first big commercial hit.

GameMaker splits a game into resources. Sprites are the pictures. Sounds are music and effects. Backgrounds are the scenery. Objects are things that can do something. And rooms are the levels and screens.
A sprite is an image, or a number of images, that represents something in the game.
If it's not animated, like a tree, it's one picture. If it is animated, it has several sub-images shown one after another, like a flip-book.
To create one, right-click Sprites and choose Create Sprite. Give it a name starting with s p r, like spr Player, then click Edit Sprite.
Make a new image, leave it at thirty-two by thirty-two pixels, and draw your player. Fill the space, because it looks very small on screen!
Then make a wall, an enemy and a key the same way. Don't spend ages perfecting them. You can improve them at the end.
And use a naming convention. S P R for sprites, O B J for objects, R M for rooms. Then spr Player and obj Player are easy to tell apart.
Page four: objects and instances. To see a sprite in the game or interact with it, you need to make it into an object.
But the object itself isn't placed into the game. It's a template. An instance is a copy of the object placed in a room.
So you could make one wall object, and place a hundred instances of it to build a maze.
Think of a cookie cutter. The cutter is the object. Every cookie you cut out is an instance.
Each object can have events. An event is something that happens in the game, like a key being pressed, two objects colliding, or the object being created.
And inside each event, you drag in actions. Actions are what the object does when that event happens.
So to make the player move: create obj Player, choose spr Player, and tick Solid. Add a Keyboard Left event, and drag in Move Fixed, set to left with speed five.
Then repeat for up, down and right.
Test yourself. You test the game and the player won't stop moving. Why, and how do you fix it?
Because nothing tells it to stop. Add a No key event, with Move Fixed, the centre square for no direction, and speed zero.
For walls, create obj Wall, tick Solid, and add a collision event with the player. A collision event runs when two instances touch. Use Move Fixed to stop the other object, which is the player.
And if the player is thirty-two pixels and the gaps are thirty-two pixels, it gets stuck. So scale the sprite to eighty percent, with horizontal and vertical both ticked so it isn't stretched.

Page seven: sound and backgrounds. Sound, also called audio, keeps players engaged. There are two main types.
Background music, which plays throughout a level and sets the mood. And sound effects, which play when something happens, like losing a life or collecting a coin.
A scream could darken the mood, while a hand clap celebrates finishing a level. And sounds tell you how you're doing without reading anything.
Backgrounds change the mood too. A dark background can make a game seem scary. A bright one makes it more child-friendly. And it should match the genre.
A genre is the style or category of a piece of work. Games are grouped by their challenges, story and gameplay, not just what they're about.
Action games involve physical challenges needing hand-eye coordination. Subgenres include platform games, like Super Mario Bros, fighting games, like Street Fighter, and shooters.
Adventure games are about solving puzzles by interacting with people or the environment, without reflex or action challenges. Like Monkey Island or Myst.
In role playing games, or R P Gs, you play adventurers who specialise in skills while following a storyline. Like Pokémon, Zelda or Final Fantasy.
Simulation games closely simulate a real or fictional reality, like The Sims or Flight Simulator. Strategy games need careful thinking and planning, like Civilization or chess.
And sports games simulate real sports, against real people or A I. Like EA Sports FC, Rocket League, or Mario Kart.
Tip: explain how a game fits its genre. Pokémon is an R P G because you control a trainer whose team gains skills as you follow a storyline.

Last page: scoring and target audience. Scoring is a quantity, usually points, linked to a player or team. Most games use it to measure success.

The target audience is the particular group of people a game is aimed at. Keep them in mind all the time, because they're the people who'll play it.
To spot it, look at the colours, the characters, the gameplay, and the PEGI age rating. Three, seven, twelve, sixteen or eighteen.
A bright cartoon puzzle game rated PEGI three is for young children. A dark, realistic shooter rated eighteen is for adults.
